measures.title: Right to Collective Bargaining
measures.subtitle: Constitutional amendment to protect workers' right to organize and collectively bargain
measures.proposedConstitutionalText: That employees have a right to organize or join a labor organization for the purpose of collectively bargaining with their employer through an exclusive representative of their choosing for the purpose of negotiating wages, hours, and working conditions and to protect their economic welfare and safety in the workplace.
measures.plainLanguageSummary: Proposal 3 would add workers' rights to organize unions and collectively bargain to the Vermont Constitution. It would also bar laws that prohibit agreements requiring union membership as a condition of employment — the kind of law usually called 'right-to-work,' which lets workers in a unionized workplace opt out of paying union dues.
whatItDoes: Adds a right for employees to organize or join a labor organization to collectively bargain with their employer, through an exclusive representative of their choosing
Covers negotiating wages, hours, and working conditions, and protecting economic welfare and safety in the workplace
Bars laws that interfere with, negate, or diminish employees' right to collectively bargain
Bars laws that prohibit employer–union agreements requiring union membership as a condition of employment
As part of the constitution, it could be changed only by a future constitutional amendment
whatItDoesNot: The text doesn't itself require anyone to join a union — but it does bar laws that would prohibit employer–union agreements requiring membership as a condition of employment
Does not force employers to agree to specific union demands
measures.argumentsDisclaimer: The following arguments are drawn from positions stated by supporters and opponents of this measure. They do not represent the views of this voter guide.

for: Supporters argue constitutional protection is harder to undo than statutory protection
Supporters cite research suggesting right-to-work policies are associated with lower wages
Supporters say Vermont's union workforce has contributed to economic stability in the state
against: Opponents argue the amendment could deter businesses from locating in Vermont
Opponents argue constitutional amendments should address fundamental rights, not labor policy
Opponents argue right-to-work laws give individual workers freedom of choice in union participation

legislativeHistory.action: Passed Vermont House with bipartisan support
Passed Vermont Senate again, unanimously (second required passage)
Passed Vermont House — certified for November 2026 ballot
Formally proclaimed by Gov. Phil Scott for the November 3, 2026 ballot

measures.context: Because this would be part of the Vermont Constitution, a future legislature couldn't change it by passing an ordinary law; it would take another constitutional amendment.

measures.title: Equal Protection of Law
measures.subtitle: Constitutional amendment adding an explicit equal rights clause to the Vermont Constitution
measures.proposedConstitutionalText: That the people are guaranteed equal protection under the law. The State shall not deny equal treatment under the law on account of a person's race, ethnicity, sex, religion, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, or national origin.
measures.plainLanguageSummary: Proposal 4 would add an explicit equal protection clause to the Vermont Constitution, listing nine protected characteristics. Vermont currently has broad general equality language in the constitution but no specific equal protection clause like the one in the 14th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.
whatItDoes: Guarantees the people equal protection under the law
Bars the State from denying equal treatment under the law on account of race, ethnicity, sex, religion, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, or national origin
States that the Article does not prevent measures intended to provide equality of treatment and opportunity for members of groups that have historically been subject to discrimination
whatItDoesNot: Does not change existing state anti-discrimination laws
Does not create new enforcement mechanisms beyond existing courts
Does not directly apply to private discrimination — only state action
Does not affect criminal or civil liability between private parties
measures.argumentsDisclaimer: The following arguments are drawn from positions stated by supporters and opponents of this measure. They do not represent the views of this voter guide.

for: Supporters say state-level constitutional protection would be independent of federal court decisions
Supporters argue the amendment would strengthen legal protections for the nine listed characteristics
Supporters say explicit constitutional language clarifies rights that may currently require legal interpretation
against: Opponents argue Vermont's existing statutory anti-discrimination laws already cover these characteristics
Opponents argue constitutional amendments could produce unintended legal interpretations by courts
Opponents point to the potential for litigation over broad terms like 'equal treatment'

legislativeHistory.action: Senate Judiciary Committee approved second passage
Formally proclaimed by Gov. Phil Scott for the November 3, 2026 ballot

measures.context: Unlike the U.S. Constitution's 14th Amendment (which guarantees equal protection at the federal level), Vermont's current constitution has no specific equal protection clause. Vermont does have Article 7 (government exists for the common benefit) and statutory anti-discrimination protections — PR.4 would add an explicit constitutional equal protection clause.

[Right to collectively bargain]" and Proposal 4 as "Article 23. [Equality of rights]". For the exact wording, read your district's sample ballot.
